body:
Choose diverse investments: Put together a diversified portfolio of short- and long-term investments at varying risk levels. You can use stocks, bonds, and mutual funds to create balance. This mix helps you manage market volatility and stay aligned with your long-term goals. [...] Here are five types of investment strategies used by investors. You can pick one or combine several to help you build a balanced portfolio that aligns with your financial goals and comfort level.

### 1. Buy-and-hold investing [...] Buy-and-hold investing focuses on long-term growth. Investors purchase assets like stocks, ETFs, and annuities and hold on to them for the long term. This approach works well for retirement planning because it encourages investors to avoid reacting to short-term market swings. It also emphasizes letting your money compound over time.

### 2. Passive index fund investing

High-yield savings accounts: 3% to 4%+.
 CDs: 3% to 4%+, depending on term.
 Bond mutual or index funds: 3% to 4% for U.S. government bonds; more for riskier bonds.
 S&P 500 (an index of U.S. large-cap stocks): 10% long-term historical average annualized return.

How do I know which investment is best for me?How do I know which investment is best for me?

When choosing an investment type, you'll want to consider your risk tolerance and how soon you'll need the money. [...] Government bonds are virtually a risk-free investment, as they’re backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. “Bonds offer a ballast to a portfolio, usually going up when stocks go down, which enables nervous investors to stay the course with their investment plan, and not panic sell," says Delia Fernandez, a certified financial planner and founder of Fernandez Financial Advisory in Los Alamitos, California. [...] ## 3. Government bonds

Bonds can offer investors a relatively safe form of fixed income. A government bond is a loan to a government entity (such as the federal or municipal government) that pays investors interest over a set period of time, typically one to 30 years. Because of that steady stream of payments, bonds are known as fixed-income securities.
